title: Keep Right to Keep Right?

source.pdf_page_offset_note: Physical page 1 is the contest summary cover; physical page 2 is printed page 1, and physical page 54 is printed page 53.

notes: All 54 local UTF-8 page text files were read in bounded physical-page ranges.
All 54 physical pages were visually reviewed through isolated byte-bounded JPEG proxies before stage generation.
No full-page original PNG, embedded base64 image, or multi-image tool result was sent through model transport.
Formula, matrix, chart, table, type-classification, and cross-reference uncertainties remain explicit warning anchors rather than silent repairs.

decisions: which rule is preferred by traffic regime

section_map.summary: The title turns a familiar keep-right phrase into a compact traffic-rule evaluation frame.
The duplicated summary states the simulation ladder, nine-rule comparison, five evaluation criteria, traffic-regime result, left-driving adaptation, intelligent control, and ramp extension.
The restatement separates overtaking simulation from multi-criteria rule evaluation and names left-driving and intelligent-system extensions.
The introduction moves from freeway performance to the keep-right decision, then positions cellular automata through a short literature review.
The assumptions exclude pedestrians, crosswind, emergency-lane use, curves, and slopes while fixing homogeneous rule-following categories.
The notation tables bind lane gaps, vehicle speeds, time steps, flow counts, experience measures, and multi-criteria quantities to stated units.
The overview connects a microscopic lane-change model, a periodic ring-road cellular automaton, and an open-boundary ramp refinement.
The basic model translates overtaking trigger, acceleration, front-gap, rear-gap, and return-lane safety reasoning into inequalities.
The extended model fixes vehicle classes, cells, speeds, probabilities, update order, lane-change laws, and periodic boundary conditions.
The refined model adds entrance and exit ramps, open boundaries, Poisson inflow, exit propensity, and failed-entry or failed-exit outcomes.
The factor study defines light and heavy traffic and compares lanes, maximum and minimum speed limits, and signaling across flow, safety, and experience criteria.
The rule study defines five basic and four improved alternatives, aligns five criteria, constructs relative deviations, and reports regime-specific preferred rules.
The sensitivity study perturbs vehicle mix, randomization probability, and willingness to change lanes by up to fifteen percent.
The discussion mirrors the model for left-driving countries, changes compliance probabilities for intelligent control, and varies ramp-exit propensity.
The final assessment credits vehicle heterogeneity, criteria, ramps, and apparent local robustness while acknowledging simplified judgment and guessed parameters.
Section conclusions convert factor and rule comparisons into different recommendations for light traffic, heavy traffic, and rush-hour operation.
The references identify cellular-automaton, traffic-engineering, fuzzy-evaluation, web, and company-data sources without supplying executable inputs or simulation code.

assumptions.summary: Pedestrians, crosswind, emergency-lane traffic, curvature, and grades can be omitted for the stated freeway simulation.
Aggressive and non-aggressive drivers follow the same relevant rule set and act from local information.
Drivers change lanes with fixed willingness probabilities, maximize their own travel progress, and use only nearby vehicles.
A 4 m by 6 m cell, 2000-cell road, one-second step, and last 1000 of 20000 steps adequately represent the modeled freeway.
Cars, buses, and trucks occur in a 60/30/10 mix with fixed occupancy and maximum speeds.
Periodic boundaries represent a repeatable long freeway section at controlled occupancy.
Open-boundary inflow is Poisson and entrance-ramp inflow is balanced in expectation with exit-ramp demand.
Coefficient-of-variation weights appropriately encode criterion importance from discrimination among alternatives.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: The summary names five performance criteria, nine rules, and separate preferred rules for light and heavy traffic.
Notation tables define vehicle states, gap variables, event counts, multi-criteria values, weights, and relative deviation.
Vehicle characteristics fix cell occupancy, maximum speed, and a 60/30/10 traffic mix attributed to a freeway-company source.
Occupancy and time-space diagrams distinguish light traffic at 0.1 from heavy traffic at 0.4 for later experiments.
Flow, speed, lane utilization, sharp braking, shifting, satisfaction, and speed variability are defined as performance criteria.
Five basic rules and four improved rules are encoded as lane-changing, lane-assignment, or lane-specific speed constraints.
Table 4 supplies the five-rule by five-criterion light-traffic matrix and the ideal alternative.
Tables 5 and 6 report relative deviations for basic rules under light and heavy traffic.
Table 7 reports nine-rule deviations and regime-specific preferred policies.
Sensitivity tables record relative output changes for vehicle mix, randomization, and lane-change willingness.

models.summary: Represent the trigger and safety logic for moving left to pass and returning right.
Simulate heterogeneous vehicles through ordered movement and lane-change updates under periodic boundaries.
Add entrance and exit ramps, Poisson inflow, exit propensity, and failed entry or exit behavior.
Measure traffic flow, safety, lane use, and driver experience for factor and rule comparisons.
Vary occupancy, lanes, speed limits, and signaling while separating light and heavy traffic results.
Encode five basic and four improved lane rules as changes to the same cellular-automaton laws.
Combine five traffic criteria and select regime-specific rules by distance from an ideal alternative.
Perturb vehicle mix, random slowing, and lane-change willingness by up to fifteen percent and record metric deviations.
Modify orientation, compliance probabilities, and p_exit to explore transfer beyond the base ring-road rule.

dependency_graph.handoff: Trigger and safety inequalities become the lane-change laws in the cellular automaton.
The movement laws are retained while periodic boundaries are replaced by explicit ramps and stochastic inflow.
Vehicle trajectories and event counts feed the flow, safety, utilization, and experience metrics.
The typed criteria are compared across controlled factor levels and traffic regimes.
Alternative policies are encoded by changing the cell and lane laws while retaining the base simulation interface.
Nine rule-specific metric vectors enter the weighted relative-deviation calculation.
The selected rule and baseline parameters define the local sensitivity experiments.
Open-boundary ramp outputs and compliance probabilities are reused in the transfer scenarios.

verification.summary: The periodic boundary explanation can be checked against constant vehicle count and occupancy control.
verification.strength: The intended density control is explicit.
verification.limitation: A short ring is only an asserted surrogate for a long open freeway.

verification.summary: Criterion formulas can be traced from vehicle events to performance dimensions.
verification.strength: Flow, safety, utilization, and experience are separated.
verification.limitation: Several extracted summations and labels require visual interpretation.

verification.summary: Factor conclusions can be compared with Figures 7-23 under light and heavy traffic.
verification.limitation: No raw trajectories, seeds, replicates, or uncertainty bars are supplied.

verification.summary: The five basic-rule rows can be recomputed from Table 4, the ideal vector, weights, and aggregate deviation.
verification.limitation: The method is called fuzzy although the displayed calculation is coefficient-of-variation weighted distance.

verification.summary: Table 7 supports the two regime-specific rule recommendations.
verification.limitation: The overall column aggregation is not explained.

verification.summary: Sensitivity tables identify the changed input and percentage response for five metrics.
verification.strength: Three uncertain parameter groups are tested.
verification.limitation: One stochastic realization or unknown replicate design cannot establish general robustness.

verification.summary: Ramp-extension figures connect p_exit to flow, speed, lane use, and failure ratio.
verification.limitation: Balancing entrance and exit counts partly constrains the observed flow behavior.

results_trace.summary: Occupancy around 0.2-0.3 is treated as the watershed between light and heavy traffic.
Lane number is reported as weak at fixed occupancy, maximum speed limit matters mainly in light traffic, and minimum speed limit mainly in heavy traffic.
Signaling is reported to reduce flow and speed while changing braking and shifting behavior.
Among five basic rules, keep-right has the smallest light-traffic deviation and lane-specific speed limits the smallest heavy-traffic deviation.
Among all nine rules, partial-assigned-lane-and-keep-right is preferred in light traffic and lane-specific speed limits in heavy traffic.
The tested plus-or-minus fifteen-percent parameter changes yield reported metric deviations up to about 16.6 percent.
Swapping lane-change willingness for left-driving transfer is reported to change criteria by at most 4.6 percent.
Intelligent control is reported to improve heavy-traffic flow while increasing shifting and changing lane utilization.
Higher p_exit lowers heavy-traffic average speed and, in the reported simulation, can lower failure to reach the exit.

contributions.summary: Separates lane-change incentive from front and rear safety conditions.
Turns the behavioral analysis into an ordered multi-lane cellular-automaton interface.
Uses periodic boundaries to control occupancy for factor comparisons.
Adds explicit ramp behavior and open boundaries as a realism extension.
Evaluates traffic rules on flow, safety, lane use, and driver-experience dimensions.
Encodes implementable alternatives through lane assignments and lane-specific speed limits.
Reports different preferred rules for light and heavy traffic rather than one unconditional policy.

visualization_observations.summary: The left-lane schematic fixes the subject vehicle, nearby vehicles, and gap directions used by the trigger and safety inequalities.
The return-right schematic distinguishes right-front and right-rear vehicles for the printed conditions.
The cellular-automaton flowchart makes the movement and lane-changing decision order inspectable.
The freeway photograph anchors the exit-before-entrance ramp geometry used by the refined model.
Time-space diagrams contrast unconstrained high-speed traces with congested low-speed traces for the light/heavy distinction.
Occupancy sweeps compare flow, speed, lane utilization, braking, shifting, satisfaction, and speed variability for three and four lanes.
Paired light/heavy plots expose the effects of maximum limits, minimum limits, and signaling across traffic metrics.
Basic-rule plots compare flow, speed, braking, satisfaction, and speed variability before aggregation.
The criterion table, ideal vector, relative-deviation matrix, and weight vector expose the multi-criteria calculation inputs.
The basic-rule deviation tables make the light/heavy preference reversal directly scannable.
The nine-rule table places light, heavy, and unexplained overall deviations beside the final recommendations.
Sensitivity tables show signed metric changes for three parameter groups across both traffic regimes.
Intelligent-system plots compare baseline, semi-intelligent, and complete control for flow, speed, braking, shifting, and lane use.
Ramp plots trace p_exit against flow, average speed, lane utilization, and failure ratio in light and heavy traffic.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: The summary previews the complete simulation-to-rule-decision route, but award status alone does not prove which feature judges valued.
The algorithm flowchart makes a complicated vehicle update sequence scannable, without proving code correctness.
The nine-rule table gives a decision-facing light/heavy contrast, without establishing external traffic-policy validity.

weaknesses.summary: The cover text reads 'Problem Chosen A' while the corpus manifest and filename classify this record as problem type B; the artifact retains manifest type B and records the source mismatch.
The summary says five improved rules, while section 7.4 defines four improved rules in addition to five basic rules.
The prose calls the occupancy time-space diagram Figure 8 while the page caption labels it Figure 6; later pages use Figure 8 for a lane-flow plot.
The printed right-front opportunity inequality repeats D_r,b,gap instead of the right-front symbol defined in the notation table.
The update equations and flowchart do not fully specify simultaneous lane-change conflict resolution or vehicle update ordering across lanes.
Open-boundary inflow, ramp-entry balance, and failed-entry handling are described in prose without a complete stochastic transition specification.
The extracted average-speed and speed-standard-deviation formulas have flattened indices and require visual source interpretation before numerical reuse.
The conclusion says signaling enhances safety although the immediately preceding discussion reports increased sharp-braking frequency.
The paper calls the aggregation fuzzy synthetic evaluation, but the displayed method uses coefficient-of-variation weights and distance from an ideal alternative without fuzzy membership grades.
The relative-deviation formula prints u_0i although the notation table and ideal vector imply a criterion-indexed u_0j; Table ?? is also an unresolved cross-reference.
The overall relative-deviation column in Table 7 is not derived or explained, so it cannot be independently reconstructed from the light and heavy columns.
The sensitivity claim lacks random seeds, replicate counts, Monte Carlo error, confidence intervals, and convergence evidence; maximum reported deviations reach about 16.6 percent.
The left-driving transfer assumes persistent asymmetric left/right lane-change willingness without empirical calibration and contains missing table references.
Ramp-flow conclusions are conditional on balancing entrance inflow with exit demand and on unreported simulation settings.
Agreement with common sense is used as validation without field trajectories, held-out data, or an external benchmark.
No executable code, frozen parameter file, initialization, raw output, seed, environment, or reproduction package is supplied.

independent_extensions.summary: Publish executable update rules with deterministic conflict resolution and cross-seed tests.
Calibrate occupancy regimes and lane-change probabilities against detector or trajectory data.
Compare the displayed relative-deviation method with explicit multi-criteria alternatives under transparent preference weights.
Report rule rankings across a continuous density range with uncertainty and rank-stability intervals.
Use variance decomposition, multiple seeds, and global sensitivity rather than single-parameter percentage tables.
Validate ramp queues, missed exits, and open-boundary flows against real merge and diverge observations.
